The Story of Anjan the Thief

Bowing to the lotus feet of the omniscient, passionless Jina, bestower of happiness, I write the story of Anjan the Thief, who illuminated the fearless aspect of right faith.

In the city of Rajgrih, in the land of Magadh, there lived a wealthy merchant named Jindatt. He was a man of great piety. He worshipped the Jina regularly, gave alms to the poor and suffering, observed the vows of a Jain layman, and remained ever peaceful and detached from worldly pleasures.

One night, on the fourteenth day of the lunar fortnight, Jindatt was standing in kayotsarga — the motionless posture of meditation — in a cremation ground at midnight. At that hour, two celestial beings arrived at the same spot. Their names were Amitprabh and Vidyutprabh. Amitprabh was a believer in the Jain dharma, while Vidyutprabh followed another faith. They had been testing each other's religions, and their debate had left them at an impasse.

Amitprabh said to Vidyutprabh, "Friend, set aside the question of testing the great monks who observe the highest conduct of the Jain dharma. But do you see that householder standing there in kayotsarga? If you have any power, try to disturb his meditation. If you can shake him from his stillness, we shall accept that your faith is the true one."

Provoked by this challenge, Vidyutprabh unleashed the most terrible and unbearable afflictions upon Jindatt. He summoned frightening visions, piercing sounds, and agonizing physical torments. Yet Jindatt did not flinch. He stood immovable as a mountain, utterly undisturbed in his meditation.

When dawn broke, both gods revealed their true forms and honoured Jindatt with great devotion. They praised him lavishly and bestowed upon him a supernatural power called the Akashgamini Vidya — the ability to travel through the sky. They told him, "O best of laymen, from this day forward this power is yours. When you impart it to others through the prescribed practice of the Panch Namaskar Mantra, they too shall acquire it." With these words, they returned to their heavenly abode.

Jindatt was overjoyed. His long-cherished wish to visit the natural, self-created Jina temples — the sacred sites not built by human hands — was at last fulfilled. That very day, using his newfound power, he flew through the sky to the eternal Jina shrines and worshipped the Jina there with boundless devotion — worship that bestows the blessings of heaven and liberation.

From that time on, Jindatt travelled daily through the sky to visit the sacred Jina temples. One day, as he was returning, he noticed a man below — a thief named Anjan — being led away in chains by the king's soldiers. Anjan had been caught in the act, and the punishment for his crimes was to be severe.

Moved by compassion, Jindatt descended from the sky and approached the soldiers. He asked them to release the prisoner into his custody, offering his own reputation and wealth as surety. The soldiers, knowing Jindatt's saintly character, agreed. Jindatt took Anjan home and, instead of punishing him, taught him the Jain dharma. He initiated Anjan into the practice of the Panch Namaskar Mantra and imparted to him the Akashgamini Vidya.

Anjan was transformed. The thief who had once stolen from others now devoted his life entirely to spiritual practice. He observed the vows with great sincerity, practised meditation with single-minded focus, and in time became a monk. As a monk, he bore every hardship without complaint and advanced steadily on the path of purification.

Through right faith, right knowledge, and right conduct, the former thief Anjan destroyed all his karmic bonds and attained liberation — the same supreme goal that had eluded him through countless births of wrongdoing. His story demonstrates that the door to liberation is open to all, regardless of one's past. Even one who has lived as a thief, when touched by true faith and guided by a compassionate teacher, can walk the path to freedom.
